title: Her onstage singing voice advanced offstage racial reform
text:
Her onstage singing voice advanced offstage racial reform
Marian Anderson was already a world-famous contralto when she was barred from singing at Washington’s Constitution Hall in 1939. Anderson was Black. The National Society Daughters of the American Revolution (DAR), the organization that owned the venue, only permitted white artists to perform there.
The blowback was swift. First Lady Eleanor Roosevelt, a member of the DAR, publicly resigned from the organization. In a letter to its president, she wrote, “You had an opportunity to lead in an enlightened way and it seems to me that your organization has failed.” In response to the controversy, Interior Secretary Harold L. Ickes, the president of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, and other luminaries arranged for Anderson to give an open-air concert from the steps of the Lincoln Memorial. An integrated crowd of 75,000 people gathered on Easter Sunday to hear her sing. Millions more tuned in to a live radio broadcast.
In his excellent biography of the singer, “Voice of a Century,” Anthony Tommasini reveals Anderson did not want to mention the historic concert in her 1956 autobiography. (She eventually relented.) “She worried that this ‘affair,’ as she had been dubbing it, would come to define her,” Tommasini writes, adding, “To a large extent that has proved true.”
A biography of Marian Anderson highlights the artistry of the Black singer’s contralto and also her contrarian approach to winning equality.
Tommasini’s sensitive account does justice to Anderson as both an accomplished musical artist and a reluctant civil rights symbol. He explains at the outset that “hers was a true, rich, and rare contralto, the lowest-set female voice.” Tommasini, previously chief classical music critic for The New York Times, writes admiringly of Anderson’s vocal instrument, whether describing its “richness and beauty” early in her career or its “greater warmth” and “earthier texture” in later years.
The eldest daughter of working-class parents in Philadelphia, Anderson began singing in church as a child. Her gifts were immediately evident. But when she attempted to enroll in a local music academy, she was told that the school did not accept Black students. The editor of an African American newspaper helped organize a fundraiser to cover private voice lessons for her.
Anderson was forced to contend with racial discrimination throughout her career. Tommasini reports that she didn’t even consider seeking roles in opera because “the field was closed to Black artists in America.” Instead, she pursued a career as a concert singer, performing as a soloist accompanied by a piano. When her accompanist Billy King arranged a tour of Black churches and colleges in the Jim Crow South in the early 1920s, they endured the indignities of segregated travel.
During the early 1930s, Anderson spent several fruitful years training in London and Berlin. With her acclaimed interpretations of German lieder (art songs), she became a sensation in Europe. (She typically concluded her recitals with a set of African American spirituals – her way of asserting that they had artistic merit equal to the European musical canon.) It’s poignant to contrast these extraordinary experiences with the humiliations that routinely confronted Anderson at home. Even in the North, when the celebrated performer stayed in hotels, her meals were served to her privately in her room. She was made aware that she wasn’t welcome in public dining rooms. “If I were inclined to be combative, I suppose I might insist on making issues of these things,” Anderson once said, adding that doing so was “not my nature.”
Albert Einstein wished otherwise. He first met Anderson in 1937, when she gave a recital in Princeton, New Jersey. When the famous physicist heard that the hotel she had reserved refused to admit her because of her race, he invited her to stay in his home. The two developed a warm friendship. Their only disagreement was that Einstein, a Jewish refugee from Nazi Germany and a strong supporter of civil rights in the United States, felt that Anderson should use her platform to speak out against racial prejudice. For her part, Anderson saw her role as modeling excellence in the hope of easing the path for the Black performers who would follow her.
By this measure, Tommasini suggests that she succeeded. In 1955, the 58-year-old Anderson at last fulfilled her lifelong dream of appearing with New York’s Metropolitan Opera, becoming the company’s first African American soloist. She played the small role of Ulrica in Verdi’s “Un ballo in maschera.”
Among those in the audience was African American soprano Leontyne Price, who, as a teenager, had sat in a segregated auditorium in Mississippi to hear Anderson sing. In 1961, Price made her own Met debut. She had a leading role. This time, Anderson was in the audience. “Without you, none of it would have been possible for me,” Price wrote to the trailblazing contralto, who died in 1993. “You paid the great price to make it easy for all of us.”
